title: Sicily — Jewel of the Mediterranean
quiz.0.question: What is the most famous volcano on Sicily?
quiz.0.explanation: Etna is Europe's most active volcano; its volcanic soils give Etna DOC wines their distinctive minerality.
quiz.1.question: Which red grape is most representative of Sicily?
quiz.1.explanation: Nero d'Avola is Sicily's most important red grape, known as "the king of Sicily".
quiz.2.question: What is the main red grape of Etna DOC?
quiz.2.explanation: Nerello Mascalese is the main red grape of Etna DOC; its elegant style is often compared to Pinot Noir.
quiz.3.question: What is Sicily's only DOCG?
quiz.3.explanation: Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG is Sicily's only DOCG, a blend of Nero d'Avola and Frappato.
slides.0.title: 🌋 Sicily (Sicilia)
slides.0.subtitle: A thousand-year wine culture on volcanic soil
slides.1.title: 🏝️ Sicily at a Glance
slides.1.content:
Italy's largest island, at the centre of the Mediterranean, facing the mainland across the Strait of Messina. The Italian region with the most vineyard area (about 100,000 ha) and among Italy's top four producers; Etna, 300 days of sunshine and a melting pot of cultures have created the Mediterranean's richest treasury of grapes.

📍
Location
The largest island in the Mediterranean; Mount Etna (over 3,300 m) in the east, the southern tip 140 km from Tunisia; capital Palermo
🌾
Vineyards
About 100,000 ha (250,000 acres), the largest vineyard area in Italy; DOC/DOCG make up only about 20% of production and Terre Siciliane IGT about 40% — still one of Italy's main bulk-wine regions
🏆
Appellations
1 DOCG (Cerasuolo di Vittoria) + 23 DOCs; a treasury of Italian native grapes, with dozens of local varieties
🌋
Volcanic wonder
Etna, Europe's highest active volcano, became Sicily's first DOC in 1968; the volcanic islands of Pantelleria and Lipari have their own DOCs too. Etna is now hailed as "the Burgundy of the Mediterranean"
slides.2.title: 🏛️ History and a Melting Pot of Cultures
slides.2.content:
Phoenicians and Greeks, the Roman Empire and the Arabs, Norman kings and English merchants — thousands of years of cultures have left a deep mark on Sicilian wine, creating one of the world's richest island wine cultures

8th c. BC
Greek colonisation: the Greeks were among the first to colonise the island; Sicily became a key centre of Magna Graecia, and they brought sophisticated viticulture and winemaking
From the 3rd c. BC
Roman Empire: the Romans replaced the Greeks and treated Sicily as "Rome's granary", focusing on cereals to feed the expanding empire
827–1061
Arab rule: irrigation and agriculture advanced, but vines were grown mainly for raisins; Sicily then flourished under the Normans (11th–13th c.)
1770s to today
The rise of Marsala and the modern revival: in the 1770s the English merchant John Woodhouse discovered the local vino perpetuo, fortified it and shipped it to England; in the 19th century Sicily mass-produced bulk wine to fill the gap left by phylloxera in Europe, turned to quality in the 1980s–90s, and Etna rose to fame in the 2000s

slides.3.title: 📜 History and the Industry Today (IWS Official Material)
slides.3.content:
Greeks → Romans
The Greeks brought sophisticated viticulture and winemaking, making Sicily a centre of Magna Graecia; the Romans who followed focused on cereals
9th–13th c.
Agriculture advanced in the Arab period (9th–11th c.), but grapes were mostly grown for raisins; Sicily flourished under the Normans (11th–13th c.)
14th–19th c.
A long economic and social decline; Marsala rose in the 18th–19th centuries; in the 19th century, as phylloxera devastated France and elsewhere, Sicily mass-produced bulk wine for Europe
20th c. → today
For most of the 20th century the focus was Marsala and bulk wine; the shift to quality came in the 1980s–90s; in 2011–2012 the island-wide Sicilia DOC was created and the former Sicilia IGT became Terre Siciliane IGT

slides.4.title: 🌍 Terroir Analysis
slides.4.content:
Living volcanic soil on Etna, Mediterranean sunshine, and elevation — three factors that give Sicily an extreme stylistic range, from elegant and mineral to rich and generous

🌋

North-east — the Etna volcano

Setting: the north, east and south slopes of Etna, 300–1,200 m; Europe's highest active volcano

Soil: volcanic ash and basalt gravel, rich in minerals (iron, potassium, magnesium), superbly free-draining

Climate: cool, with wide day–night swings and more rain than the rest of the island; temperature drops 0.6°C per 100 m of altitude

Hallmarks: the contrada system (like Burgundy's climats) and ungrafted century-old bush vines (alberello)

☀️

South — Mediterranean sunshine

Setting: south-eastern hills and coastal plains around Noto, Pachino and Vittoria

Soil: sand, clay and limestone; deep soils with good water retention

Climate: hot and dry with 300+ days of sun; the Sirocco, a hot African wind from the south-east, affects the south and west; sea breezes moderate locally

Hallmarks: the best home of Nero d'Avola — fully ripe, rich fruit, high alcohol

🗺️ Sicily's four terroir zones

slides.5.title: 🗺️ Geography, Climate, Soils and Viticulture (IWS Official Material)
slides.5.content:
📍
Location
36°–38°N; Italy's largest region and the largest island in the Mediterranean. The Strait of Messina separates it from Calabria and the Canale di Sicilia from North Africa; at the centre of the Mediterranean, it is a crossroads of cultures. Historically divided into Val di Mazara (west), Val Demone (north-east) and Val di Noto (south-east)
⛰️
Topography
A vast area with very varied topography, geology and climate: the Sicilian Apennines in the north (Peloritani, Nebrodi, Madonie), the Monti Iblei plateau in the south-east and Etna in the east; significant volcanic activity (Etna, Stromboli, Vulcano)
☀️
Climate
Mediterranean, becoming moderate Mediterranean to semi-continental at altitude; low rainfall; the Sirocco, a warm African wind from the south-east, affects the south and west
🪨
Soils
Clay and limestone in the hills, sand along the coast; volcanic soils on Etna, Pantelleria and the Aeolian Islands (Lipari, Salina, Stromboli), varying widely in age and composition

🍇 Grape mix

White grapes 60%+
mostly white in the west
mostly red in the east
Native/traditional 80%
international about 20%
International varieties
introduced in the 1980s, expanded in the 1990s–early 2000s; Chardonnay and Syrah lead, mostly in the west

✂️ Training: alberello (frequently tested)

Tradition: alberello bush vines

Sicily's historic training system, ideal for a hot, sunny, dry environment: low yields and high sugar and extract. On Etna each alberello vine has its own stake.

Modernisation

In the 1980s–90s an EU vineyard modernisation programme removed much alberello; today Guyot and cordone speronato (spur-pruned cordon) account for 80% of plantings, and traditional alberello for less than 10%.
slides.6.title: 🍇 Native Grapes in Depth
slides.6.content:
🔴 Nero d'Avola — the king of Sicily

Origin: officially called Calabrese, named after the town of Avola in the province of Siracusa; Sicily's most widely planted red grape

Aromas: black cherry, blackberry, plum, chocolate, sweet spice, tobacco

Structure: deep colour, smooth tannins, high alcohol, fresh acidity, a good match for oak; traditionally bush-trained (alberello)

Range: from everyday wine to 15-year-old single-vineyard bottlings, with huge quality differences; comparable to Syrah / Cabernet Sauvignon

🔴 Nerello Mascalese — the soul of Etna

Home: a native grape of Etna's slopes, 80%+ of Etna red wines

Aromas: red cherry, raspberry, rose, herbs, volcanic minerality, smoke

Structure: pale to medium colour, smooth tannins, high alcohol, lively acidity; late-ripening and able to express individual sites, in a style like Pinot Noir / Nebbiolo

Ageing: top single-contrada wines age 10–20 years; Nerello Cappuccio is the supporting grape that adds colour

⚪ White grapes — Grillo, Carricante, Catarratto

Grillo: a natural cross of Catarratto × Zibibbo, a traditional Marsala grape; modern dry whites are fresh, with lemon, white peach and almond, best at 2–5 years

Carricante: the backbone of Etna whites, high acidity and minerality, old vines age 5–10 years — the essence of basalt soils

Catarratto: Sicily's most widely planted grape, neutral and fresh, for everyday wines; Inzolia is floral with Mediterranean herbs

Zibibbo: Moscato d'Alessandria on Pantelleria, made into golden passito with honey and apricot
slides.7.title: 🍇 Native Grapes: The Full Picture (IWS Official Material)
slides.7.content:
⚪ White grapes

Catarratto Bianco

Sicily's most widely planted grape, historically used for Marsala; two main biotypes: Catarratto Bianco Comune and the higher-quality Catarratto Bianco Lucido.

Grillo

A natural cross of Catarratto Bianco × Zibibbo, used for Marsala and dry whites. Traditional dry wines were dark, nutty and prone to oxidation; modern ones are fresh and clean, with body and texture. The name comes from the Sicilian dialect "grilli" (grape pips).

Inzolia (Ansonica)

Historically grown in the west for Marsala; now made into varietal dry wines or blends, usually picked early to keep acidity.

Carricante

A high-quality native grape historically grown on Etna's slopes, often above 900 m; high in malic acid with pronounced minerality and moderate acidity; the main grape of Etna Bianco, often from very old ungrafted vines.

Zibibbo

The Sicilian name for Muscat of Alexandria, from the Arabic "zabib" (raisin); thick-skinned with large, fleshy berries, ideal for passito and also eaten fresh or as raisins; widely planted on volcanic Pantelleria.

Malvasia di Lipari

Historically grown on the volcanic Aeolian Islands; genetically identical to Malvasia di Sardegna and Calabria's Greco Bianco; used for the renowned Malvasia delle Lipari Passito.

🔴 Red grapes

Nero d'Avola (Calabrese)

Officially Calabrese, Sicily's most widely planted red grape, traditionally bush-trained (alberello); deep colour, smooth tannins, high alcohol, fresh acidity and an affinity with oak.

Nerello Mascalese

Etna's noble native grape, late-ripening and able to express the nuances of each site; pale to medium colour, complex and refined aromas, smooth tannins, high alcohol and lively acidity. Many Etna vines are ungrafted and over a century old; recent research names its parents as Sangiovese × Mantonico Bianco. Often paired with Nerello Cappuccio.

Frappato

Historically grown around the town of Vittoria in the south-east and traditionally blended with Nero d'Avola; bright ruby, fragrant, fresh and juicy, with medium body and tannins.

Other reds

Perricone (Pignatello), Nocera (Faro DOC), Nerello Cappuccio (Etna, Faro).
slides.8.title: 🏆 Three Core Appellations
slides.8.content:
From the slopes of Europe's highest active volcano to the Mediterranean plains, Sicily's three flagship appellations each have their own style, showing the island's diversity

🌋 Etna DOC

The north, east and south slopes of Europe's highest active volcano, 300–1,200 m. Nerello Mascalese (red) + Carricante (white). Elegant, high acidity, mineral, with a contrada culture. Hailed as "the Burgundy of the Mediterranean". €15–200+.

🏅 Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG

Sicily's only DOCG (2005), around Vittoria in the south-east. A blend of Nero d'Avola 50–70% + Frappato 30–50%. Medium body, ripe cherry, balanced and elegant. Top producers: COS / Arianna Occhipinti. €15–45.

🍷 Marsala DOC

The port of Marsala at the western tip; in the 1770s the English merchant Woodhouse took it to England. Made from Grillo, Catarratto and Inzolia and fortified with grape spirit. Categories range from Fine (1 year) to Vergine Riserva (10+ years), from dry to sweet, for cooking and drinking. €8–60+.

slides.10.title: 🌋 Etna Slope by Slope
slides.10.content:
Etna's vineyards lie on the volcano's north, east and south slopes, across 20 villages and 133 contrade — the north slope is the most celebrated, and its finely divided contrade are as sought after as Burgundy's climats

🧭 North slope (Versante Nord) — the heart
About 600–1,000 m, less rain than the east and south, cool summers and wide day–night swings; around Randazzo, Castiglione di Sicilia, Linguaglossa and Passopisciaro, mainly Nerello Mascalese reds, home to star estates such as Passopisciaro and Terre Nere
🧭 East slope (Versante Est) — facing the sea, wettest
Facing the Ionian Sea, the rainiest and most humid side; the village of Milo is the only source of Etna Bianco Superiore (min. 80% Carricante), and its Carricante whites are fresh, mineral and saline
🧭 South slope (Versante Sud) — warm and sunny
Warmer and sunnier, with vineyards climbing above 1,000 m; riper fruit and fuller body. In the 1990s Benanti and winemaker Salvo Foti led the renewed focus on Etna's terroir and native grapes here
📜 Etna DOC rules
Etna Rosso: min. 80% Nerello Mascalese, max. 20% Nerello Cappuccio; Riserva min. 4 years (1 in wood). Etna Bianco: min. 60% Carricante, max. 40% Catarratto; there are also Rosato and Spumante. When all the grapes come from one official contrada, its name may appear on the label
slides.11.title: 🌋 Etna DOC: History and Terroir (IWS Official Material)
slides.11.content:
19th c.
The province of Catania (including Etna) was one of Sicily's most widely planted and productive areas; in the late 19th–early 20th centuries it focused on bulk wine, and it declined for most of the 20th century
1968
Etna DOC is created — Sicily's first DOC
1990s → 2010s
In the 1990s Benanti and Salvo Foti began focusing on Etna's terroir and native grapes; in the 2000s producers finally put Etna on the world map; the 2010s brought investment and new estates; in 2011 the 133 contrade were officially adopted as MGAs
🗺️ What is a contrada?

A small geographic sub-division, similar to a hamlet or neighbourhood. Sicilian vineyards have always been identified by contrada; in 2011 Etna DOC officially adopted the historic contrada map, registering them as MGAs (Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive) that may appear on labels — 133 contrade across 20 villages.

⛰️ High-altitude climate

Vineyards at 300–1,200 m, with cool conditions, wide day–night swings and more rainfall than most of Sicily; harvest runs from the end of September to the end of October, one of the latest in Italy.

🪨 Volcanic soils and old vines

Dark, loose volcanic sand over a lava subsoil resists phylloxera, so many old vines are ungrafted. The terrain is rugged, with small, often terraced parcels held up by stone walls, traditionally planted as alberello with one stake per vine.

🏛️ The palmento

Etna's traditional winery built of black lava stone, with vats on several connected levels so that gravity moves the must between foot-treading, fermentation and ageing. Some natural-wine estates (such as Vino di Anna) still use one.

⚪ Etna Bianco and Superiore

Etna Bianco: min. 60% Carricante, max. 40% Catarratto (other whites max. 15%), and many are 100% Carricante; mostly made in stainless steel, some in large oak casks; mineral, racy and long-lived. Etna Bianco Superiore: min. 80% Carricante, all from the village of Milo on the east slope.
slides.12.title: 🧬 Sicily's Two Great Reds Compared
slides.12.content:
Sicily's two great reds — Nero d'Avola and Nerello Mascalese embody opposite philosophies of style, two extremes of Sicilian wine

👑 Nero d'Avola — power

Home: Noto / Pachino in the south-east (hot coast)

Colour: deep purple-red, almost black

Aromas: blackberry, prune, chocolate, sweet spice, leather

Structure: smooth tannins, full body, high alcohol, fresh acidity

Comparable to: Syrah / Cabernet Sauvignon

Ageing: 5–15 years for the best, plus everyday drink-now styles

🌋 Nerello Mascalese — elegance

Home: Etna's north slope (cool, high altitude)

Colour: pale ruby, orange at the rim

Aromas: red cherry, rose, herbs, volcanic minerality, smoke

Structure: fine tannins, high acidity, medium body

Comparable to: Pinot Noir / Nebbiolo

Ageing: top contrada wines 10–20 years

🍷 A third way: the golden blend of Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG

Nero d'Avola (50–70%) + Frappato (30–50%) — power meets freshness. Nero d'Avola brings structure and depth, Frappato light floral and strawberry energy; together they give Sicily's only DOCG its unique character. Cerasuolo means "cherry-coloured" in Italian, a perfect description of its colour.
slides.13.title: 🍷 The Marsala Fortified-Wine Tradition
slides.13.content:
In the 1770s English merchants brought the local vino perpetuo to the world, founding the Mediterranean's greatest fortified-wine tradition — once ranked with Port and Sherry as one of the three great fortified wines, Marsala is now on the road to a fine-wine revival

1770s
Onto the world stage: John Woodhouse discovered the local vino perpetuo in Marsala, refined and fortified it and shipped it to England; purchases by the Royal Navy (Nelson) during the Napoleonic Wars made it famous
1833–1880
Golden age: Benjamin Ingham improved production and became the most successful exporter; from the 1830s Sicilian merchants such as Florio emerged, and Marsala stood alongside Port and Sherry as one of the three great fortified wines
21st c.
Fine-wine revival: pioneers such as Marco De Bartoli revived traditional Vergine Marsala and the perpetuum solera system, restoring its value as a fine wine

Three key Marsala ageing categories — complexity through time

🍷 Fine (entry)

Min. 1 year (8 months in wood), 17.5% ABV, straightforward fruit, often used in cooking (tiramisu, zabaglione)

A kitchen staple, €8–15

⏳ Superiore Riserva (step up)

Min. 4 years in wood, 18% ABV, good complexity with almond, hazelnut and honey, for sipping

For tasting, €20–40

🏆 Vergine Riserva (top)

Min. 10 years in wood (also called Stravecchio), 18% ABV, fortified only with no sweetening additions, may use a solera; the highest dry category

For collectors, €40–80+
slides.14.title: 🍷 Marsala Rules, Grapes and Styles (IWS Official Material)
slides.14.content:
1770s → 1830s
Woodhouse refined and fortified vino perpetuo for export to England; Benjamin Ingham became the most successful exporter; in the 1830s Sicilian merchants such as Florio emerged
1860s → 1950s
Annexation to the Kingdom of Italy favoured local producers; phylloxera gradually eroded quality; in 1931 the government officially delimited the zone; in the 1950s flavoured "Marsala Speciali" became popular, damaging the image of quality Marsala
1969 → today
Marsala DOC was approved in 1969; stricter rules in 1984 finally excluded Marsala Speciali; today production is aimed mostly at the low-end market and the food industry, but a few quality producers remain (such as Marco De Bartoli)
🍇 Grapes and area

Classic Marsala is a white fortified wine from white grapes: Grillo, Catarratto, Inzolia (Ansonica), Damaschino (Carricante is not among them); the rarer Rubino (ruby) is made from Nero d'Avola, Perricone and Nerello Mascalese. The zone is a large area at Sicily's western corner, with vineyards on flat coastal land and low hills, a fully Mediterranean climate, and some of the driest, hottest conditions on the island.

🏆 Marsala Vergine (Solera)

Fortified only with grape spirit or alcohol — no other additions allowed. Min. 5 years in wood, 10 for Riserva (Stravecchio); some producers use a solera; min. 18% ABV and under 4% residual sugar; may be vintage-dated or a blend of vintages. Considered the most authentic style, closest to the ancient vino perpetuo; the best are dry, intense and complex, but it is a tiny share of production.

🍯 Marsala Superiore and Fine (conciati)

Both developed in the 19th century and, besides fortification, may receive "concia": mosto cotto (cooked must), sifone (fortified grape must, mistella) or mosto concentrato (concentrated must). They are classed by colour — Ambra (amber), Oro (gold), Rubino (ruby) — and by sweetness — secco, semisecco, dolce. Superiore: min. 18% ABV, min. 2 years in wood (Riserva 4), under 20% of production, complex and velvety; Fine: min. 17.5% ABV, min. 1 year (8 months in wood), mostly for the food industry.
slides.15.title: 🏅 Other Key Appellations and Sicilia DOC (IWS Official Material)
slides.15.content:
🍒 Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG & Vittoria DOC

Timeline: Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOC in 1973 → DOCG in 2005, when Vittoria DOC was also created; the area includes a tiny part of the nearby Riesi DOC known for excellent Nero d'Avola.

Terroir: coastal and inland hills with a fully Mediterranean, hot and arid climate; sand and clay over limestone with pockets of iron-rich terra rossa.

Rules: Nero d'Avola 50–70% (colour, body, tannin) + Frappato 30–50% (lightness, acidity, fresh floral and fruit aromas), min. 13% ABV, with a Classico sub-zone. Vittoria DOC covers varietal Frappato, Inzolia and Nero d'Avola plus Rosso and Novello; some of the best varietal Frappato comes from here.

🍇 Eloro DOC — home of Nero d'Avola

Flat coastal land and low hills in the south-eastern corner, with dark, gravelly calcareous soils; grapes are Nero d'Avola, Frappato and Perricone (Pignatello), and varietal Nero d'Avola must be at least 90%. The official sub-zone Eloro Pachino: min. 80% Nero d'Avola, max. 20% Frappato and/or Perricone; Riserva needs 2 years of ageing (6 months in wood).

🌊 Faro DOC

A historic zone near Messina, DOC since 1976 and revived by the Palari estate in the 1990s. Steep slopes right by the sea, with alluvial soils (more clay on the Tyrrhenian side, more sand on the Ionian side) over a metamorphic subsoil. The only area besides Etna where Nerello Mascalese and Nerello Cappuccio are traditional: Nerello Mascalese 45–60%, Nerello Cappuccio 15–30%, Nocera 5–10%.

⛰️ Contea di Sclafani DOC

An inland zone with full continental influence, a wide diurnal range and medium- to high-altitude vineyards. The Rosso is Nero d'Avola and/or Perricone, the Bianco Catarratto; both come in Riserva and Vendemmia Tardiva (late-harvest) versions.

🏝️ Sicilia DOC & Terre Siciliane IGT

Until 2011 many quality wines were labelled under the regional Sicilia IGT; in 2012 Sicilia IGT was elevated to Sicilia DOC and replaced by Terre Siciliane IGT. Sicilia DOC has stricter rules and must be bottled on the island; many of Sicily's best wines use it. Terre Siciliane IGT can be bottled off the island, but Nero d'Avola and Grillo cannot be produced under this IGT.
slides.16.title: 🏝️ Volcanic-Island Sweet Wines: Pantelleria and Lipari (IWS Official Material)
slides.16.content:
🌬️ Pantelleria — Zibibbo on the island of the wind

📜 History

Strongly influenced by Arab culture, with a long tradition of air-drying Zibibbo for raisins and sweet passito; passito became popular in the 19th–20th centuries and Passito di Pantelleria became a DOC in 1971. In the 20th century merchants controlled production and quality fell; a few producers such as De Bartoli, Murana and Donnafugata led a revival in the 1980s; in 2013 it became Pantelleria DOC, an umbrella for several Zibibbo-based styles.

🌋 Terroir and the alberello pantesco

Jagged, irregular hills of volcanic origin (cuddie), with terraces held up by dry-stone walls of volcanic rock; vines and capers are almost the only viable crops, on sand and porous volcanic gravel. The climate is fully Mediterranean, hot and arid, and strong, persistent winds dehydrate the grapes, interrupt ripening and cut yields, so vines are trained very low in shallow hollows (conche) and surrounded by volcanic stone walls (giardino pantesco). This "alberello pantesco" is inscribed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage.

🍯 Passito vs Moscato di Pantelleria

Passito di Pantelleria: two harvests — some Zibibbo is picked in August and dried in the sun, the rest is picked, pressed and fermented, and the dried grapes are then added to the must; min. 14% ABV, golden to amber, luscious, with tropical fruit, dried and candied fruit, honey and spice. Moscato di Pantelleria: made from fresh (sometimes over-ripe) Zibibbo without drying — paler, less sweet, lower in alcohol and fresher. There are also spumante, frizzante, dry Zibibbo, Moscato Liquoroso and Passito Liquoroso (liquoroso = fortified).

🌬️ The Aeolian Islands — Malvasia delle Lipari DOC

📜 History

Named after Aeolus, Greek god of the winds; vines have been grown here since the Greeks settled in the 6th century BC. The sweet wines were highly reputed in the 19th century, declined in the 20th and were revived in the 1980s by producer Carlo Hauner.

🌋 Area and wines

Mountainous volcanic islands with small, sometimes terraced plots on shallow sandy volcanic soils, mostly on the island of Salina. 92–95% Malvasia di Lipari + 5–8% Corinto Nero. Malvasia delle Lipari Passito: late-harvested grapes that are also dried — golden-amber, intense and complex; Malvasia delle Lipari: late-harvested but not dried — lighter and less sweet.
slides.17.title: 🏰 Notable Producers
slides.17.content:
Etna cult estates, Cerasuolo's natural-wine pioneers and top Nero d'Avola producers — six benchmark Sicilian wineries

PP
Master of Etna contrade
Passopisciaro — Est. 2000

Tuscan estate owner Andrea Franchetti came to Etna and pioneered single-contrada wines, vinifying each plot separately to show the volcano's microclimates.

🌋 Contrada series (C / P / R / S / G), 100% Nerello Mascalese, mineral and elegant, €50–150+
High on Etna's north slope × contrada philosophy × top attention from Wine Advocate / Decanter
DF
Face of modern Sicily
Donnafugata — Est. 1983

The Rallo family's flagship, with estates at Contessa Entellina, Pantelleria, Vittoria (Acate) and Etna (Randazzo), while the historic Marsala cellar handles ageing and bottling — modern and traditional in balance.

🍷 Mille e Una Notte (top Nero d'Avola) €60–80 / Ben Ryé (top Passito di Pantelleria) / Sul Vulcano Etna range
Estates across the island × a modern fine-wine approach × world-famous passito
COS (Cerasuolo pioneer)

Founded in 1980, a biodynamic pioneer that revived amphora fermentation; a benchmark for Cerasuolo di Vittoria Classico

Cerasuolo di Vittoria Classico Amphora
Frappato / Pithos range
€18–40 / natural and lively
Arianna Occhipinti (queen of natural wine)

Founded in 2004 with a minimal-intervention philosophy; SP68 is a must-try for natural-wine lovers worldwide — light, lively and fresh

SP68 Frappato + Nero d'Avola
Il Frappato / Siccagno Nero d'Avola
€18–35 / fresh and natural
💚 Entry

€8–18

Nero d'Avola DOC, Grillo Sicilia DOC, entry-level Etna Rosso — easy-drinking Mediterranean charm

🧡 Step up

€18–50

Etna Rosso Contrada, the Donnafugata range, Cerasuolo Classico — a leap in quality, great for entertaining

❤️ Collector

€50–200+

Passopisciaro Contrada series, Mille e Una Notte, Terre Nere Prephylloxera — top wines for the cellar
slides.18.title: 🍽️ Food and Wine Pairing
slides.18.content:
Sicilian food meets Sicilian wine — Mediterranean ingredients, Arab spice influences and sweet seafood, each dish with its ideal Sicilian partner

🔴 Nero d'Avola

With: caponata (Sicilian sweet-and-sour aubergine)
A traditional sweet-and-sour dish of aubergine, tomato, olives and pine nuts. Nero d'Avola's black fruit and spice echo this quintessentially Mediterranean classic.

🌋 Nerello Mascalese (Etna Rosso)

With: wild mushroom and truffle risotto
Ingredients from volcanic soil: Etna Rosso's elegant minerality and fine tannins are a natural match for the earthy flavours of mushrooms — a pairing from the same volcanic land.

⚪ Grillo / Carricante (white)

With: Sicilian grilled swordfish (spada)
Sicily's signature seafood. The wine's fresh acidity suits the firm fish, and its lemon and almond notes harmonise with a tomato-mint sauce — pure Mediterranean.

🍯 Passito di Pantelleria (sweet)

With: cannoli / cassata siciliana (Sicilian desserts)
The apricot and honey of sun-dried Zibibbo blend beautifully with creamy ricotta — a textbook case of pairing sweet with sweet.
slides.19.title: 🔥 The Modern Sicilian Quality Revolution
slides.19.content:
🔬 Sicily's quality revolution

From bulk-wine source of southern Italy to fine-wine star — in the 2000s the rescue of Etna's old vines, Cerasuolo's natural-wine movement and the rise of Pantelleria's sweet wines drove Sicily's quality revolution together and redrew the map of Italian wine

Three paths that brought Sicily back to the world stage

🌋 The rise of Etna (2000s)

Newcomers such as Andrea Franchetti arrived on Etna, a single-contrada culture took shape around ungrafted century-old bush vines, and Wine Advocate scores of 90+ became common

International recognition as "the Burgundy of the Mediterranean"

🌱 The organic and natural-wine movement

300 days of sun and a dry climate naturally limit disease; Sicily has the largest organic vineyard area in Italy, COS revived amphora winemaking, and Arianna Occhipinti led the trend

Italy's largest organic vineyard area

🍯 Passito di Pantelleria

The volcanic island of Pantelleria (closer to Tunisia than to Sicily), sun-dried Zibibbo, and Donnafugata's Ben Ryé — the world's best-known passito, golden with apricot and honey

Sicily's sweet-wine calling card

slides.21.title: 🎓 Key Takeaways
slides.21.points.0: ✓ Sicily has the largest vineyard area in Italy (about 100,000 ha), ranks among Italy's top four producers, and has 1 DOCG + 23 DOCs; Terre Siciliane IGT accounts for about 40%
slides.21.points.1: ✓ Etna (Europe's highest active volcano) became Sicily's first DOC in 1968; its distinctive mineral wines have earned it the name "the Burgundy of the Mediterranean"
slides.21.points.2: ✓ Nero d'Avola (king of Sicily, rich black fruit and spice) and Nerello Mascalese (soul of Etna, elegant and mineral) are the two signature reds
slides.21.points.3: ✓ Etna's vineyards lie on the north, east and south slopes (the north most celebrated); since 2011 the 133 contrade may appear on labels; ungrafted century-old bush vines
slides.21.points.4: ✓ Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG is Sicily's only DOCG (2005), a balanced blend of Nero d'Avola + Frappato
slides.21.points.5: ✓ Marsala DOC: in the 1770s John Woodhouse fortified vino perpetuo and shipped it to England; Vergine is fortified only, with no concia; categories run from Fine (1 year) to Vergine Riserva (10 years), and a solera may be used
slides.21.points.6: ✓ Top estates: Passopisciaro & Terre Nere (Etna cult wines), Donnafugata (fine wines across the island), COS & Arianna Occhipinti (natural-wine pioneers)
slides.21.points.7: ✓ Passito di Pantelleria: a sweet wine from sun-dried Zibibbo; the volcanic island's alberello pantesco is UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage
slides.21.points.8: ✓ White grapes make up over 60% (white in the west, red in the east) and native/traditional grapes about 80%; Catarratto is the most planted, and Grillo is a Catarratto × Zibibbo cross
slides.21.points.9: ✓ Sicilia DOC (2011–2012) must be bottled on the island; Terre Siciliane IGT cannot be used for Nero d'Avola or Grillo
slides.21.points.10: ✓ Faro DOC (Nerello Mascalese, Cappuccio, Nocera), Eloro DOC (Pachino sub-zone, Nero d'Avola) and Malvasia delle Lipari DOC are also must-know appellations
slides.21.points.11: ✓ The 2000s quality revolution: the rise of Etna, the organic and natural-wine movement (Italy's largest organic vineyard area), top wines at €50–200+
slides.22.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
slides.22.questions.0.question: Why is Etna called "the Burgundy of Italy"?
slides.22.questions.0.options.0: A. It also grows Pinot Noir
slides.22.questions.0.options.1: B. It emphasises differences between hillside plots (contrade) and a refined, elegant terroir
slides.22.questions.0.options.2: C. Its climate is the same as Burgundy's
slides.22.questions.0.explanation: Thanks to its unique volcanic soils, high altitude (300–1,200 m) and a philosophy built on the differences between contrade, Etna makes refined, elegant reds from Nerello Mascalese — hence "the Burgundy of Italy".
slides.22.questions.1.question: Which best describes the style of Nero d'Avola?
slides.22.questions.1.options.0: A. Light, low in alcohol, delicately fruity
slides.22.questions.1.options.1: B. High tannin and acidity, like Barolo
slides.22.questions.1.options.2: C. Rich and generous, with ripe black fruit and chocolate
slides.22.questions.1.options.3: D. Sweet and low in acidity, for drinking young
slides.22.questions.1.explanation: Nero d'Avola ripens fully in Sicily's heat, giving deep-coloured, generous reds with ripe blackberry, prune, chocolate and spices such as cinnamon — Sicily's most representative grape.
slides.22.questions.2.question: Which of these are well-known Sicilian native white grapes? (Select all that apply)
slides.22.questions.2.explanation: Grillo (used for Marsala and dry whites), Catarratto (Sicily's most planted) and Carricante (Etna whites) are all Sicilian native white grapes. Sangiovese is a Tuscan red grape.
slides.22.questions.3.question: What kind of wine is Marsala?
slides.22.questions.3.explanation: Marsala is Sicily's famous fortified wine, fortified with grape spirit or alcohol (Fine min. 17.5%, Superiore and Vergine min. 18%). In the 1770s the English merchant John Woodhouse refined the local vino perpetuo and fortified it for export to England, making it famous.
slides.22.questions.4.question: Which statements about Etna DOC are true? (Select all that apply)
slides.22.questions.4.options.0: A. It lies on the slopes of an active volcano
slides.22.questions.4.options.1: B. Its main red grape is Nerello Mascalese
slides.22.questions.4.options.2: C. It has attracted great international attention in recent years
slides.22.questions.4.options.3: D. All its wines are sweet
slides.22.questions.4.explanation: Etna DOC lies on the slopes of the active Etna volcano and makes refined reds from Nerello Mascalese, highly praised in recent years by Wine Spectator, Decanter and others. Etna makes mainly dry wines, not sweet ones.
slides.22.questions.5.question: Grillo is a natural cross of which two grapes?
slides.22.questions.5.explanation: IWS: Grillo is a natural cross of Catarratto Bianco and Zibibbo (Muscat of Alexandria), used for Marsala and fresh modern dry whites.
slides.22.questions.6.question: Which of the following is NOT a grape used to make Marsala?
slides.22.questions.6.explanation: Classic Marsala uses Grillo, Catarratto, Inzolia (Ansonica) and Damaschino; Carricante is the main grape of Etna Bianco.
slides.22.questions.7.question: What does "contrada" mean on an Etna label?
slides.22.questions.7.options.2: C. A category of bulk wine
slides.22.questions.7.explanation: A contrada is a small geographic sub-division, similar to a hamlet or neighbourhood. In 2011 Etna DOC officially adopted 133 historic contrade as MGAs that may appear on labels.
slides.22.questions.8.question: Which vine-training system was historically used in Sicily?
slides.22.questions.8.explanation: Alberello (bush vine) suits a hot, dry environment, with low yields and high sugar and extract; but an EU modernisation programme removed much of it in the 1980s–90s, and today Guyot and cordone speronato account for 80% of plantings, alberello for less than 10%.
slides.22.questions.9.question: What does "liquoroso" on a label indicate?
slides.22.questions.9.options.2: C. A wine made with concentrated grape must
slides.22.questions.9.explanation: Liquoroso means a fortified wine, for example Moscato di Pantelleria Liquoroso or Passito Liquoroso. Cooked must is mosto cotto and concentrated must is mosto concentrato.
